title: WHY DOES LEVITICUS FORBID SEX WITH YOUR MOTHER-IN-LAW?
paragraphs: WHY DOES LEVITICUS FORBID SEX WITH YOUR MOTHER-IN-LAW?
The Disturbing Command Most Christians Skip Over—And the Stunning Reason It Still Matters
There are verses in the Bible people underline.
There are verses people memorize.
There are verses printed on coffee mugs, stitched onto pillows, posted over sunsets, and whispered in hospital rooms.
And then there is Leviticus 20:14.
Most people don't put this one on the refrigerator.
“And if a man take a wife and her mother, it is wickedness…”
It is uncomfortable.
Strange.
Severe.
Maybe even disturbing.
And if we are honest, when many Christians reach passages like this during their yearly Bible reading plan, their eyes start moving a little faster.
Genesis feels alive.
Psalms feels beautiful.
The Gospels feel familiar.
Then Leviticus arrives…
…and suddenly you're reading laws about blood, nakedness, forbidden relatives, sacrifices, uncleanness, and sexual relationships you never imagined needing a commandment against.
Then comes this:
A woman and her mother.
Why?
Why would God need to say this?
Why would Scripture specifically prohibit a man from sexually taking both a woman and her mother?
And perhaps an even more uncomfortable question:
What does an ancient command like this have to do with you?
More than you might think.

Because beneath this strange prohibition is something profoundly relevant to every marriage, every family, every temptation, every secret browser history, every forbidden attraction, every shattered boundary, and every human heart that has ever whispered:
“What if nobody finds out?”
Stay with me.
Because this isn't really an article about your mother-in-law.
It is about boundaries.
It is about desire.
It is about what happens when desire refuses to recognize that some doors were never meant to be opened.
And ultimately…
it is about why sinners like us desperately need Jesus Christ.
First, we need to correct something that is often lost in the provocative way this question is phrased.
Leviticus 18:17 does not literally use the English expression “mother-in-law.”
The Hebrew reads:
“עֶרְוַת אִשָּׁה וּבִתָּהּ לֹא תְגַלֵּה”
Transliterated:
“ʿErwat ʾishshah uvitah lo tegalleh.”
In straightforward English:
“You shall not uncover the nakedness of a woman and her daughter.”
The passage continues by prohibiting taking her son's daughter or daughter's daughter sexually as well, explaining:
“שַׁאֲרָה הֵנָּה זִמָּה הִוא”
“Sha'arah hennah; zimmah hi.”
They are close relatives.
It is “zimmah.”
That Hebrew word matters.
זִמָּה — zimmah.
Depending upon context and translation, it carries the idea of depravity, lewdness, wickedness, or an outrageous sexual violation.
This isn't Scripture acting embarrassed about sexuality.
The Bible isn't embarrassed by sex.
God invented it.
Genesis presents the union of husband and wife before humanity ever fell into sin.
The problem in Leviticus isn't that sexuality exists.
The problem is sexuality crossing a boundary God established.
Then Leviticus 20:14 makes the family relationship behind our question unmistakable:
“וְאִישׁ אֲשֶׁר יִקַּח אֶת־אִשָּׁה וְאֶת־אִמָּהּ זִמָּה הִוא”
In essence:
If a man takes a woman and her mother, it is zimmah.
That second woman is his wife's mother.
His mother-in-law.
So yes—the prohibition is real.
But the reason behind it reaches much deeper than an isolated rule about one particularly disturbing relationship.
God was drawing a line around the family.
Think about that.
Your family is supposed to contain relationships in which sexuality is simply not an option.
A daughter should be able to exist around her father without wondering whether his eyes are evaluating her sexually.
A sister should be able to trust her brother.
A mother should not become her daughter's sexual competitor.
A son should not have to wonder whether his father desires his wife.
A wife should not have to wonder whether bringing her mother into her home means bringing another potential sexual rival into her marriage.
Family should contain places where desire stops.
Where people are allowed to simply be family.
Where love does not have to become erotic.
Where affection does not become possession.
Where closeness does not become permission.
Where vulnerability is protected rather than exploited.
And suddenly Leviticus doesn't sound quite so primitive.
It sounds painfully perceptive.
Because one of fallen humanity's oldest lies is this:
If I desire something strongly enough, perhaps I have a right to it.
Scripture says no.
Desire is not lord.
Jesus is.
Your feelings are real.
But they are not God.
Your attractions may be powerful.
But they are not sovereign.
Your body can want something your soul must refuse.
And sometimes holiness sounds like one simple sentence:
That person is not mine to take.
There are boundaries that love respects precisely because love is love.
And that is why this command reaches far beyond the bizarre scenario people laugh about when they first encounter it.
God was protecting distinctions.
Marriage matters.
Family matters.
Kinship matters.
Sexual boundaries matter.
Other people are not objects placed on earth to satisfy whatever desire happens to rise inside us.
That truth becomes especially piercing in a culture where desire is often treated as identity and restraint can be treated as repression.
Scripture presents another vision.
Freedom isn't doing everything you desire.
Sometimes freedom is finally becoming strong enough to say no to the thing that has been controlling you.
Jesus said something terrifyingly perceptive about sin.
The problem is not merely “out there.”
It comes from within.
Christ taught that sexual immorality, adultery, greed, deceit and other evils proceed from the human heart.
That means Leviticus eventually brings us somewhere uncomfortable.
Not merely to ancient Israel.
Not merely to someone else's scandal.
To us.
Because maybe you have never desired your mother-in-law.
But have you ever desired someone else's spouse?
Have you ever entertained fantasies about someone God has not given you?
Have you ever secretly enjoyed attention that should have been shut down?
Have you ever kept a conversation alive because you liked how it made you feel?
Have you ever deleted messages because you knew your husband or wife would understand immediately what you were pretending wasn't happening?
Have you ever said, “We're just friends,” while knowing something inside you had already crossed a line?
Have you ever watched pornography while convincing yourself that because no physical affair happened, nobody was betrayed?
Have you ever protected a secret desire more carefully than you protected your marriage?
Maybe your scandal has never become public.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe your spouse doesn't know.
Your pastor doesn't know.
Your children don't know.
Your church doesn't know.
Maybe the person sitting beside you every Sunday thinks everything is fine.
But God knows.
And this is where people often misunderstand biblical conviction.
God exposes darkness not because He delights in destroying sinners.
He exposes darkness because darkness destroys sinners.
A surgeon doesn't reveal a tumor because he hates the patient.
He reveals it because leaving it hidden could kill them.
And Scripture cuts because Scripture is trying to bring us to truth.
But then something breathtaking happens.
The Bible does not end in Leviticus.
The story keeps moving.
Through sacrifice.
Through covenant.
Through prophets.
Through kings.
Through rebellion.
Through judgment.
Through promises.
Until eventually…
a Child is born.
The Word becomes flesh.
Jesus Christ enters our scandal.
John describes Him as being full of “grace and truth.”
Notice what Scripture refuses to separate.
Grace.
And truth.
Truth without grace can become condemnation without hope.
Grace without truth becomes permission without transformation.
Jesus brings both.
He does not look at sexual sin and pretend it isn't sin.
But neither does He look at the repentant sinner and say redemption is impossible.
And that is where this article stops being merely about forbidden relationships.
Because somewhere reading this is someone carrying sexual shame.
Something happened.
Something you did.
Something someone did to you.
Something you watched.
Something you hid.
Something you participated in.
Something you wish you could erase.
Maybe you crossed boundaries knowingly.
Maybe someone violated yours.
And those are not morally identical things.
If someone abused, coerced, groomed, manipulated, or assaulted you, their sin against you is not transformed into your guilt merely because it involved your body.
But perhaps you were the one who crossed the line.
Then Scripture doesn't invite you to rename darkness.
It invites you to repent.
And repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is the doorway home.
Paul wrote to Christians in Corinth who came from deeply sinful backgrounds, including sexual immorality.
Then came four words carrying enough grace to resurrect a human life:
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
Past tense.
Then Paul says they were washed.
Sanctified.
Justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of God.
That is Christianity.
Not:
“I never had a scandal.”
But:
“My scandal does not get the final word.”
Not:
“I was always clean.”
But:
“Jesus washed me.”
Not:
“I never wandered.”
But:
“The Shepherd came looking for me.”
Not:
“I deserved another chance.”
But:
“Grace found me anyway.”
This is why Gospel Warrior keeps returning to the same truth:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
The Cross does not declare your sin harmless.
The Cross declares your sin so serious that the Son of God shed His blood for sinners—and His mercy so astonishing that sinners who come to Him in repentance and faith can be forgiven.
That is grace.
Costly grace.
Blood-bought grace.
Grace that doesn't merely cover yesterday.
Grace that begins transforming tomorrow.
So perhaps the deepest question isn't:
“Why would Leviticus forbid sex with your mother-in-law?”
Perhaps the deeper question is:
Why does the human heart keep wanting to cross boundaries God created for our good?
And an even greater question follows:
What does God do with people who already crossed them?
Look at Jesus.
That is the answer.
Bring Him the hidden browser history.
Bring Him the affair.
Bring Him the fantasy.
Bring Him the emotional entanglement you've been calling friendship.
Bring Him the secret messages.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the years you cannot undo.
Bring Him the marriage you wounded.
Bring Him the heart you allowed to wander.
Bring Him everything.
Not because sin doesn't matter.
Because the blood of Christ does.
Repentance means turning.
It means no longer defending what God is asking you to surrender.
It can mean ending the secret conversation.
Deleting the number.
Confessing the lie.
Seeking wise pastoral help.
Installing accountability.
Repairing what can responsibly be repaired.
Fleeing temptation instead of negotiating with it.
And where crimes, abuse, coercion, or exploitation are involved, repentance must never be used as a substitute for protecting victims or appropriate legal accountability.
Grace is not concealment.
Grace brings us into the light.
Perhaps that is what somebody needed today.
Not another inspirational quote.
Not another religious performance.
Truth.
Maybe you've been hiding so long that hiding started feeling normal.
Come into the light.
Jesus already knows what is behind the door.
And He is still calling you.
If this exposed something you've been hiding from God, you don't need to write the details publicly.
And if Christ has already brought you out of something you once believed would destroy your life, don't hide the testimony forever.
Someone reading the comments may desperately need evidence that grace still changes people.
“Christ is still healing me.”
Because someone you know may be quietly losing a war nobody knows they are fighting.
Someone's marriage may be one message away from disaster.
Someone may be rationalizing an attraction that needs to die before it destroys three generations of relationships.
Someone may be drowning in sexual shame and assuming Jesus wants nothing to do with them.
Let truth travel farther than temptation.
Because temptation has a strange way of making yesterday's convictions disappear when tonight's desires become loud.
Come back when you need the reminder:
Not everything you desire belongs to you.
Not every door should be opened.
Not every feeling should be obeyed.
And no repentant sinner is beyond the reach of Jesus Christ.

If Gospel Warrior has been helping you understand difficult Scripture, confront sin without abandoning grace, heal through biblical truth, and grow deeper in Jesus Christ, consider staying close to this ministry.
God is not for sale.
Grace is not for sale.
The Gospel is not for sale.
But Scripture does teach believers to give willingly, deliberately, generously, and joyfully toward Gospel work.
Send it privately to someone who needs it.
Because the world doesn't need Christians who pretend they never struggled.
It needs Christians who know where to run when they do.
It needs marriages worth protecting.
Families with boundaries.
Churches where truth can be spoken without destroying the repentant.
Believers who know the difference between temptation and permission.
Men and women willing to say:
“My desires are not my god.”
And sinners who discover that the most scandalous thing in their story was not how far they fell…
but how far Jesus came to bring them home.
You may have crossed a boundary you can never uncross—but at the Cross, Jesus can still write a future your past could never deserve.
